Table~\ref{tab:ablation} separates arithmetic correctness from predictive usefulness. Development selection set the edit penalty to zero in every configuration except Intel and set both penalties to zero in S32N. The positive Intel cost penalty did not change test average precision at the displayed precision. These findings do not support the claim that every score term is needed. A single-edge cost is constant within a fixed graph, so it cannot improve the order of edges in that window.

The spread penalty had a practical threshold effect on controlled SKAB windows. Gain alone had false-positive fraction 0.613 at nominal 5\%, compared with 0.050 for the selected score. Fault recall also fell from 0.637 to 0.013. Conservatism here does not imply accurate diagnosis.

\textcolor{red}{Secondary inference ablations are still running in this layout draft.}

The production audit independently recomputed 8736 candidate scores from saved samples across 1092 cases. The largest absolute arithmetic discrepancy was 7.11$\times10^{-15}$. This verifies implementation, not the research hypotheses. Figure~\ref{fig:equations} examines paired variants, sampling variability, contaminated conditioning and measured runtime.
